text: So far we've talked about events — the dice sum to 7, the customer churns. Data science works with numbers: revenue per customer, orders per week, days until a delivery arrives. A random variable connects the two — it assigns a number to each outcome of a chance process. This lesson covers expected value and variance, finishing Chapter 2 by showing how probability turns into an average you can reason about and simulate.

A discrete random variable takes countable values — 0, 1, 2, and so on — and its distribution is a probability mass function listing P of X equals x for each value, with probabilities summing to 1. A continuous random variable can take any value in a range, like delivery time; any single exact value has probability 0, and instead a probability density function describes areas under a curve — the subject of Chapter 3.

Suppose X is the number of orders a customer places in a week: P of 0 is 0.30, P of 1 is 0.35, P of 2 is 0.20, P of 3 is 0.10, and P of 4 is 0.05 — summing to 1. The expected value is each value weighted by its probability, summed up, and it comes out to 1.25 orders per week.

Notice 1.25 isn't a value X can actually take. Expected value is a long-run average, not a prediction for any single customer, and not necessarily the most likely outcome — here the single most likely value is actually 1. Variance is the expected squared distance from the mean, using the same weighting, and comes out to 1.2875, giving a standard deviation of about 1.13 orders.

scipy's rv_discrete wraps a pmf and gives you mean, var, std, pmf of a specific value — 0.2 for exactly 2 orders — and cdf, 0.85 for the chance of 2 orders or fewer. Simulating 100,000 customers drawn from this pmf gives a mean of 1.25298 and variance of 1.29474, landing close to the theoretical 1.25 and 1.2875 — the law of large numbers at work again.

Three rules you'll use constantly. Linearity: E of a times X plus b equals a times E of X plus b. If each order brings 40 dollars and there's a 5 dollar weekly fee, revenue equals 40 X minus 5, with expected value 40 times 1.25 minus 5, equals 45 — confirmed directly from the pmf too.

Sum of expectations: E of X plus Y equals E of X plus E of Y, always, even if X and Y are dependent — for one die E is 3.5, so two dice sum to an expected 7. Sum of variances only adds up if X and Y are independent — simulating two independent customers gave a variance of the sum around 2.575, matching 2 times 1.2875.

A raffle ticket costs 5 dollars with a 1-in-30 chance of winning 100 dollars. Expected net gain: 100 times one-thirtieth minus 5, equals negative 1.67 dollars per ticket. Simulating a million tickets gave an average of negative 1.6752 — on average you lose money, which is exactly why a business running the raffle profits.

Expected value guides repeated decisions like ad campaigns, pricing, and fraud review, but it has limits — it ignores risk, since two options with the same expected value can have very different spread, and it assumes you can play many times, which a one-shot bet with a small chance of ruin violates. To recap: a random variable turns outcomes into numbers, expected value is the probability-weighted average, and linearity makes combining them easy. Chapter 3 starts with the standard discrete distributions that show up again and again.
